questions.stem: Marketing is best described as:
options: identifying customers' needs, then attracting and keeping customers profitably
the process of advertising products on television, on radio and through social media
the selling of goods to customers once production has been completed
the legal process of registering a brand name and logo with the government
questions.explanation: Marketing covers every activity involved in finding out what customers need and meeting those needs in a way that is profitable, from research to pricing, distribution and promotion. Advertising is only one part of promotion, which is itself one part of marketing.

questions.stem: Why is establishing a customer base important for achieving business objectives?
options: A large customer base guarantees that the business's costs will fall in every year.
Customers decide the objectives that the business is legally required to meet.
Regular customers provide the sales revenue needed to meet objectives such as profit and growth.
A loyal customer base removes any need for the business to set objectives of its own.
questions.explanation: Without customers there are no sales, so a stable customer base underpins objectives such as profit, market share and growth. Owners and managers, not customers, set the business's objectives.

questions.stem: A new Launceston bakery's objective is to reach $500,000 in sales in its first year. Which marketing action best supports this objective?
options: reducing its opening hours so that its weekly staff costs are lower
changing its legal structure from a sole trader to a company
spending its whole budget on new ovens rather than promotion
promoting a weekly loyalty offer to encourage repeat customers
questions.explanation: A sales objective is supported by marketing that brings customers back regularly, such as a loyalty offer. Cutting opening hours reduces costs but also reduces the chance to make sales, and a change of structure is not a marketing action.

questions.stem: Brand identity refers to:
options: the registration number allocated to a business by ASIC when it registers its business name
the total number of customers who have bought from a business since it opened
the number of different products that a business sells in each of its markets
the visible elements, such as name, logo and colours, that make a business recognisable
questions.explanation: Brand identity is how a business presents itself, through elements such as its name, logo, colours and style, so that customers recognise it and associate it with particular values. A registration number has no role in how customers perceive a brand.

questions.stem: Which is an internal factor affecting a new business's ability to establish a customer base?
options: the skills of its staff in serving customers
the level of consumer confidence in the economy
a competitor's newly launched loyalty program
changing community attitudes to sugary drinks
questions.explanation: Staff skills are within the business and under management's control, so they are an internal factor. Consumer confidence and community attitudes are macro factors, and a competitor's program is an operating factor.

questions.stem: A new Wollongong gym builds its brand around being 'the friendliest gym in town', but a larger competitor with lower fees opens next door. Which statement best analyses the situation?
options: A macro factor threatens its customer base, so it should abandon its brand at once and match the lower fees.
The competitor is an internal factor, so the gym can control its effect on the gym's customer base.
Brand identity becomes irrelevant once a rival charges less, because customers compare only price.
An operating factor threatens its customer base, so its service-based brand identity matters even more.
questions.explanation: A competitor is part of the operating environment, and a clear point of difference such as friendly service gives customers a reason to stay despite lower fees elsewhere. Many customers weigh service and experience as well as price.

questions.stem: Which is a data collection technique used in market research?
options: a SWOT analysis of the business
a Business Activity Statement
a job specification for a role
an online customer survey
questions.explanation: Surveys, interviews, focus groups and observation are techniques for collecting market research data. A SWOT analysis is a planning tool that uses information rather than a way of collecting it from customers.

questions.stem: A new café records how many people walk past its window each hour and how many of them come in. This data collection technique is:
options: a focus group
an interview
secondary research
observation
questions.explanation: Watching and recording what people actually do is observation, a primary research technique. No questions are asked, so it is not an interview or focus group, and the café is collecting the data itself rather than using published data.

questions.stem: A survey of 400 Ballarat residents finds that 60% of those aged 18–34 and 20% of those aged 55 and over would use a meal-kit delivery service. The most valid conclusion is that the business should:
options: abandon the idea, because some of the people surveyed were not interested in it
focus its first marketing on people aged 18–34, who showed the most interest
target people aged 55 and over, because they are likely to have higher incomes
expect 60% of all Ballarat residents to become regular customers of the service
questions.explanation: The data shows much stronger interest among younger respondents, so they are the logical first target market. The 60% figure applies only to the 18–34 group and to stated interest, so it cannot be applied to the whole population as regular customers.

questions.stem: Why should a new business analyse and interpret its market research data, rather than simply collect it?
options: Collected data is always reliable, so analysis is needed only by large firms.
Analysis turns raw data into findings that can guide marketing decisions.
Analysis is a legal requirement before any advertising is allowed to run.
Interpreting the data guarantees that each new product will succeed.
questions.explanation: Raw data only becomes useful when it is organised and interpreted to show patterns, such as which segment is most interested. Good analysis improves decisions, but it cannot guarantee success.

questions.stem: Market segmentation is:
options: dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics or needs
selling the same product in exactly the same way to every customer in the whole market
dividing a business into functional departments such as finance and marketing
calculating the share of total market sales that is held by each competitor
questions.explanation: Segmentation groups customers by shared characteristics, such as age, location, lifestyle or buying behaviour, so marketing can be tailored to them. Selling the same way to everyone is mass marketing, the opposite approach.

questions.stem: A Noosa surf-apparel brand targets customers who see themselves as adventurous and environmentally conscious. This segment is based on:
options: psychographic characteristics
geographic characteristics
socio-demographic characteristics
behavioural characteristics
questions.explanation: Psychographic segmentation groups customers by lifestyle, values, attitudes and personality, such as being adventurous or environmentally conscious. Demographic segmentation uses measurable traits such as age and income.

questions.stem: A business targets families with children under five who live in Melbourne's outer suburbs. Which bases of segmentation is it using?
options: demographic and psychographic
demographic and geographic
psychographic and behavioural
behavioural and geographic
questions.explanation: Family type and children's ages are demographic characteristics, and living in the outer suburbs is a geographic characteristic. Nothing in the description concerns customers' values or buying behaviour.

questions.stem: A new live-music streaming service targets people who already buy concert tickets at least twice a year. This segment is based on:
options: demographic characteristics
psychographic characteristics
behavioural characteristics
geographic characteristics
questions.explanation: Behavioural segmentation groups customers by what they do, such as how often they buy or use a product. How often people buy concert tickets is purchasing behaviour, not a measure of age, location or personal values.

questions.stem: A Hobart business makes gluten-free, vegan birthday cakes for a small group of customers at premium prices. Compared with a mass-market bakery, its approach is best described as:
options: undifferentiated marketing, treating all customers the same way
penetration pricing, setting low prices to gain market share
niche marketing, serving a narrow segment with specialised needs
mass marketing, because most households buy birthday cakes
questions.explanation: Niche marketing targets a small, clearly defined segment with specific needs, often at premium prices. Mass and undifferentiated marketing aim at the whole market, and premium prices are the opposite of penetration pricing.

questions.stem: Which consumer trend would most support demand for a new subscription meal-kit business?
options: more households wanting convenient home-cooked meals
more consumers choosing to shop for food in person every day
falling use of online shopping and home delivery
more people preferring to eat out at restaurants
questions.explanation: Meal kits offer the convenience of delivered ingredients with the appeal of cooking at home, so this trend increases demand. Falling online shopping or a shift to eating out would reduce demand for delivered kits.

questions.stem: The 7Ps of marketing are product, price, place, promotion and:
options: packaging, persuasion and public image
partners, performance and premises
people, physical evidence and process
planning, profit and positioning
questions.explanation: The 7Ps model extends the original four Ps with people, physical evidence and process, which are especially important for services. The other sets contain marketing-related words but are not part of the model.

questions.stem: In the 7Ps model, 'place' refers to:
options: the physical appearance of the business's premises
the stage that the product has reached in its life cycle
the location of the business's head office building
how and where the product is distributed to customers
questions.explanation: Place covers distribution: the channels and locations through which customers obtain the product, such as shops, websites or wholesalers. The look of the premises is physical evidence, a separate P.

questions.stem: A new Fitzroy restaurant chooses fresh flowers, spotless bathrooms and well-designed menus. Which of the 7Ps does this address?
options: physical evidence
process
place
promotion
questions.explanation: Physical evidence is the tangible environment and items customers see, which signal the quality of a service before and during the experience. Process is the set of steps by which the service is delivered.

questions.stem: A new online pharmacy simplifies its ordering and payment steps so customers can finish a purchase in under two minutes. Which of the 7Ps is it improving?
options: process
people
price
physical evidence
questions.explanation: Process refers to the procedures and flow of activities by which a product or service is delivered, such as ordering and payment. Making these steps faster and easier improves the customer's experience.

questions.stem: Why is 'people' an important element of the marketing mix for a hairdressing salon?
options: People refers to the salon's suppliers, who decide which products it is able to stock.
People matters only for businesses that sell goods online rather than in person.
Staff deliver the service, so their skills and manner shape each customer's experience.
People refers to the number of customers, which determines the prices the salon charges.
questions.explanation: In a service business the staff are part of what the customer buys, so their skill, friendliness and presentation directly affect satisfaction. In the 7Ps, people means everyone involved in delivering the product, especially staff.

questions.stem: A new technology company sets a high price for an innovative product at launch, aiming at early adopters, and lowers the price later. This pricing strategy is:
options: price skimming
penetration pricing
cost-plus pricing
loss-leader pricing
questions.explanation: Price skimming starts high to earn large margins from customers keen to buy first, then lowers the price to reach more of the market. Penetration pricing does the opposite, starting low to win market share.

questions.stem: A new energy drink enters a crowded market at a low price to win market share quickly, planning to raise the price later. Which risk is most associated with this strategy?
options: The product cannot legally be promoted while its price is set low.
A low price is unlawful in a market that has many competitors.
Customers may resist later price rises, and early profit margins are low.
The high launch price may deter all but a small number of keen early adopters.
questions.explanation: Penetration pricing sacrifices margin at first, and customers attracted by the low price may switch brands when it rises. A high launch price deterring buyers is a risk of price skimming, not penetration pricing.

questions.stem: Which is an example of promotion in the 7Ps?
options: the training of front-desk staff
a social media advertising campaign
the choice of courier for deliveries
the design of the checkout process
questions.explanation: Promotion is how a business communicates with customers to inform and persuade them, such as through advertising, sales promotions and public relations. Couriers relate to place, checkout design to process and staff training to people.

questions.stem: In which stage of the product life cycle are sales usually low and profits often negative?
options: introduction
growth
maturity
decline
questions.explanation: At introduction few customers know about the product, while development and launch promotion costs are high, so losses are common. Profits usually begin as sales rise in the growth stage.

questions.stem: Sales of a new reusable coffee cup are rising quickly, and competitors are launching similar cups. The product is most likely in the:
options: introduction stage
maturity stage
decline stage
growth stage
questions.explanation: Rapidly rising sales and competitors entering the market are typical of the growth stage. In maturity, sales level off and competition is at its most intense.

questions.stem: In the maturity stage of the product life cycle, a business is most likely to:
options: spend heavily on making customers aware that the product exists at all
withdraw the product immediately because its sales have begun to fall
set a high skimming price to target the earliest adopters of the product
differentiate its product and compete strongly on price and promotion
questions.explanation: In maturity, sales have peaked and many competitors share the market, so businesses defend their share through differentiation, pricing and promotion. Building basic awareness and skimming prices belong to the introduction stage.

questions.stem: Sales of a Melbourne company's portable DVD players have been falling for three years. It begins marketing them as compact players for caravans and boats. This is best described as:
options: an introduction-stage strategy, since the product itself has been redesigned
withdrawal from the market, since the product has reached the decline stage
an extension strategy, finding a new market for a product in decline
a growth-stage strategy, since the product has re-entered the growth stage
questions.explanation: An extension strategy, such as finding a new use or a new market, aims to lengthen the life of a product whose sales are falling. The product itself has not changed, so this is not a new introduction, and the company is not withdrawing it.

questions.stem: A product's annual sales are: year 1, 2,000 units; year 2, 9,000; year 3, 20,000; year 4, 21,000; year 5, 20,500. In year 5 the product is most likely in the:
options: decline stage
maturity stage
growth stage
introduction stage
questions.explanation: Sales rose rapidly to year 3 and have since levelled off, which is the pattern of the maturity stage. The small fall in year 5 is not yet a sustained decline, and growth would show sales still rising strongly.

questions.stem: A customer loyalty program aims to:
options: reward repeat purchases so customers keep buying from the business
reduce the business's need to provide good customer service
collect customers' details in order to sell them to other businesses
set the business's prices below those of every competitor
questions.explanation: Loyalty programs, such as points or a free item after a set number of purchases, give customers a reason to return. They support good service rather than replacing it, and selling customers' details would breach their trust.

questions.stem: Why is quality customer service especially valuable for a new business?
options: It allows the business to charge any price it likes without ever losing any of its customers.
It means the business no longer needs to promote itself in any other way.
It is required by law under the National Employment Standards.
Satisfied customers return and recommend the business, building its customer base.
questions.explanation: A new business has no reputation yet, so good service creates repeat customers and word-of-mouth recommendations. Service is one part of the marketing mix and does not remove the need for sensible pricing or promotion.

questions.stem: A new Geelong café gives a free coffee after every nine purchases, but long waits and rude service are common. Which evaluation is most valid?
options: The program may bring some repeat visits, but poor service is likely to undermine loyalty.
The program guarantees loyalty, so the quality of the café's service no longer matters at all.
The café should end the program, because loyalty programs never work in hospitality.
Long waits show strong demand, so the café's customer relations must already be good.
questions.explanation: A loyalty reward can encourage return visits, but customers who experience poor service are likely to go elsewhere regardless of the reward. Effective customer relations combine incentives with consistently good service.

questions.stem: Search engine optimisation (SEO) is:
options: paying a search engine to place ads at the top of its search results
sending regular promotional emails to a list of existing customers
using artificial intelligence to answer customers' questions online
improving a website so that it ranks higher in unpaid search results
questions.explanation: SEO improves a website's content and structure so search engines rank it higher in organic, unpaid results. Paying for ads at the top of results is paid search advertising, a separate strategy.

questions.stem: A new Adelaide bike shop uses data analytics on its online sales. Which is the most likely benefit?
options: guaranteeing that every advertisement the shop runs will lead to a sale
replacing any need for the shop to carry out market research of its own
identifying which products sell to which customers, so marketing can be targeted
removing the shop's obligation to protect its customers' personal information
questions.explanation: Data analytics finds patterns in customer and sales data, such as who buys what and when, so the business can tailor products and promotions. Using data increases rather than removes the responsibility to protect it.

questions.stem: An online clothing store uses artificial intelligence to recommend items based on each shopper's browsing history. This is mainly intended to:
options: meet the requirements of the Spam Act
set the store's prices for each season
personalise offers and increase sales
reduce the cost of delivering each order
questions.explanation: AI recommendation tools suggest products each shopper is likely to want, making the experience more personal and encouraging extra purchases. They do not affect delivery costs or legal obligations about email.

questions.stem: Compared with a newspaper advertisement, a key advantage of social media marketing for a new business is that it:
options: reaches only customers who already know about the business and its products
can target specific segments and allows two-way interaction with customers
guarantees that negative comments about the business can never appear online
costs nothing in staff time to create, post and manage the business's content
questions.explanation: Social media lets a business aim content at chosen segments and respond to customers directly, building relationships. It also exposes the business to public criticism and takes time to manage well.

questions.stem: A new business's marketing email is opened by 40% of recipients, but only 1% of recipients make a purchase. The most valid conclusion is that:
options: the subject line attracts interest, but the offer or content needs to be improved
email marketing does not work for this business and should be abandoned
the business should buy a much larger email list without getting consent
40% of the recipients bought a product as a result of opening the email
questions.explanation: A high open rate shows the email is getting attention, so the weak point is what happens after opening, such as the offer or the call to action. Opening an email is not the same as buying, and sending to people without consent breaches the Spam Act.

questions.stem: Public relations is best described as:
options: the legal process for resolving disputes between two businesses
the training given to new staff on how to provide customer service
managing communication to build and protect a positive reputation with the public
paid advertising that promotes a product's features and its current price
questions.explanation: Public relations (PR) manages how a business communicates with its customers, the media and the community in order to maintain goodwill. Unlike advertising, PR coverage such as news stories is not directly paid for.

questions.stem: A new Perth solar installer sponsors a local school's science fair and issues a media release about it. This is an example of:
options: a customer loyalty program
search engine optimisation
planned public relations
crisis public relations
questions.explanation: Planned PR consists of proactive activities, such as sponsorships, events and media releases, designed to build a positive image. Crisis PR is a response to a negative event that threatens the business's reputation.

questions.stem: How does public relations support a business's objectives?
options: Public relations guarantees that the media will report only positive stories.
Public relations removes any need for the business to advertise its products or services.
Public relations is used only after a crisis, so it plays no role in objectives.
A positive reputation builds trust, which helps attract customers and increase sales.
questions.explanation: Good PR builds goodwill with customers and the community, supporting objectives such as sales, market share and a strong reputation. PR includes planned activities, not just responses to crises, and it cannot control what the media reports.

questions.stem: Several customers of a new Brisbane restaurant fall ill after eating there. Which crisis public relations response is most appropriate?
options: respond quickly, take responsibility, explain what is being done and keep people informed
say nothing publicly until all investigations are complete, so as to avoid admitting fault
deny any link to the restaurant and suggest the customers' illness had some other cause
remove any online reviews that mention illness so that other customers do not see them
questions.explanation: Effective crisis PR is fast, honest and open, showing concern for those affected and explaining the steps taken to fix the problem. Silence, denial or hiding reviews tends to damage trust further when the facts emerge.

questions.stem: What is the most likely implication if a business fails to maintain a positive relationship with its customer base?
options: an automatic fine from the ACCC for having poor customer relations
higher sales, because unhappy customers return to the business to complain in person
a legal requirement to change its business name and its logo
a loss of customers and reputation, leading to lower sales and profit
questions.explanation: Customers who feel badly treated go elsewhere and may tell others, so sales and the business's reputation suffer. The ACCC enforces consumer law, but there is no fine simply for poor customer relations.

questions.stem: Green marketing is:
options: advertising that uses green colours and nature imagery
marketing that is aimed only at first-time customers
promoting products based on their genuine environmental benefits
marketing that is aimed at customers living in rural areas
questions.explanation: Green marketing promotes real environmental features of a product or business, such as recycled materials or lower emissions. Using green colours without any real benefit behind them is not green marketing and may mislead customers.

questions.stem: A new Sydney detergent brand labels its product 'eco-friendly' without any evidence to support the claim. This is known as:
options: psychographic segmentation, which targets environmental values
planned public relations, which builds a positive reputation
greenwashing, which may breach the Australian Consumer Law
green marketing, which the ACCC encourages every business to use
questions.explanation: Greenwashing is making environmental claims that are false, vague or unsupported, which can be misleading conduct under the Australian Consumer Law. Genuine green marketing must be backed by evidence.

questions.stem: A new online retailer wants to share its customer list with a partner business for marketing. Which approach best reflects corporate social responsibility?
options: share the list freely, because the customers' data belongs entirely to the retailer
tell customers how their data will be used, and share it only with their consent
share the list quietly, because customers rarely read the retailer's privacy policy
sell the list to the highest bidder and use the money to offer customers lower prices
questions.explanation: Protecting customer privacy means being open about how personal information is used and respecting customers' choices. Sharing data without consent may breach privacy law and would damage trust if customers found out.
